Erfundene Daten, kleine Wörterbücher. In: Made-up data, small dictionaries. In Kali: hashcat & john against your OWN test hashes.
leak.txt ist ein (erfundener) Passwort-L: leak.txt is a (made-up) password leak in plaintext – with many repeats. Which password appears most often? That is exactly what an attacker tries first.
sort stellt gleiche Zeilen untereinander: sort groups identical lines together, uniq -c counts them.
sort leak.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr | hea: sort leak.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -1 shows the most common one.
Lösung: sort leak.txt | uniq -c | sort -: Solution: sort leak.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -1 → cat befunde/talheim2026.txt
ziel.txt enthält einen UNGESALZENEN SHA-: ziel.txt contains an UNSALTED SHA-256 hash of a password. woerter.txt is a small dictionary. Which word matches? Without a salt this is done in seconds.
Hash holen: grep ziel ziel.txt | cut -d:: Get the hash: grep ziel ziel.txt | cut -d: -f2
Für jedes Wort: echo -n \"$w\" | sha256s: For each word: echo -n "$w" | sha256sum and compare with the target hash.
Lösung: H=$(grep ziel ziel.txt | cut -d:: Solution: H=$(grep ziel ziel.txt | cut -d: -f2); for w in $(cat woerter.txt); do echo -n "$w" | sha256sum | grep -q $H && echo $w; done → cat befunde/WORT.txt
leak-a.txt und leak-b.txt stammen aus zw: leak-a.txt and leak-b.txt come from two different (made-up) hacks – each email;hash. One person uses the SAME password in both (same email, same hash). This is exactly how an attacker pivots from one leak to the next.
Hängt man beide Dateien aneinander, steh: If you concatenate both files, the duplicate line appears twice.
cat leak-a.txt leak-b.txt | sort | uniq: cat leak-a.txt leak-b.txt | sort | uniq -d shows exactly that line.
Lösung: cat leak-a.txt leak-b.txt | sort: Solution: cat leak-a.txt leak-b.txt | sort | uniq -d (the email is at the front) → cat befunde/NAME.txt (the part before the @)
passwoerter.txt: Beispielpasswörter. Ang: passwoerter.txt: sample passwords. Attackers first test the pattern “capital letter + word + year” (e.g. Sommer2026). How many passwords follow exactly this pattern? The number is the file name.
grep -E nutzt erweiterte reguläre Ausdrü: grep -E uses extended regular expressions. ^ and $ mean start/end of line.
grep -E '^[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]{4}$' passwoer: grep -E '^[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]{4}$' passwoerter.txt finds the pattern, wc -l counts.
Lösung: grep -E '^[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]{4}$': Solution: grep -E '^[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]{4}$' passwoerter.txt | wc -l → cat befunde/ZAHL.txt
tempo.csv: verfahren;versuche_pro_sekund: tempo.csv: method;guesses_per_second (how fast an attacker can guess). Which method is the fastest – and therefore the worst for passwords?
sort -t\";\" -k2 -nr sortiert nach der 2: sort -t";" -k2 -nr sorts by the 2nd column as a number, descending.
head -1 nimmt den schnellsten, cut -d\";: head -1 takes the fastest, cut -d";" -f1 the name.
Lösung: sort -t\";\" -k2 -nr tempo.csv |: Solution: sort -t";" -k2 -nr tempo.csv | head -1 | cut -d";" -f1 → cat befunde/md5.txt
konfig.csv: dienst;bcrypt_runden. Mehr R: konfig.csv: service;bcrypt_rounds. More rounds = slower = safer. One service has far too few rounds (below 10). Which one?
awk -F\";\" trennt an den Semikolons; $2: awk -F";" splits on the semicolons; $2 is the number of rounds.
